title: PlantVillage Nuru helps Busia County cassava farmer Josephine Arisat select clean cuttings; she reports yields rising from 0.5 kg to 2-5 kg per plant
summary: PlantVillage's own 23 Mar 2020 post: after 18 months using Nuru, introduced via Self Help Africa and Ugunja Resource Center, Arisat reports 2.0-5.0 kg per plant against 0.5 kg; no independent source.
account: A PlantVillage (Pennsylvania State University) blog post dated 23 March 2020, the date used here, linked from the CGIAR Platform for Big Data in Agriculture's project page as a 'Success story from a cassava farmer in Busia County, Kenya', profiles Josephine Arisat of Asing'e location, Busia County, who has grown cassava since 1995 and had been using the PlantVillage Nuru smartphone app 'for a period of One and a half years' after organizations 'such as SHA and Ugunja Resource Center' introduced it. She is quoted: 'Initially, I used to harvest rotten cassava tubers whereas their leaves looked healthy. I never knew that Cassava leaves can showcase diseases', and that with Nuru she can scan leaves for cassava mosaic disease, cassava green mite or cassava brown streak disease and get management advice. The post states that before Nuru she 'would harvest just 0.5kg per Cassava plant' and that, using the app to select healthy cuttings to replant, 'she harvests between 2.0-5.0 kg per Cassava plant'; it also records that she switched in 2016 to certified seed (MM06 and Mygeria varieties), joined an aggregation selling to True Trade in 2019, and recommends one-meter spacing, none of which the post separates from the app's effect. The CGIAR page says Nuru was tested in Busia County 'in partnership with Self Help Africa, a charity helping 28,000 farmers in the cassava value chain' and that over 100 lead farmers there received smartphones at the start of 2019. Mrisho et al. (Frontiers in Plant Science, 2020), co-authored by PlantVillage and IITA developers, measured Nuru's symptom-recognition accuracy (65% in 2020 versus 40-58% for extension agents and 18-31% for farmers, including 50 farmers from Busia County) and report no individual outcomes. Business Insider (10 August 2022) independently quotes a Kilifi County farmer, Caroline Dama Kitsao, that with Nuru 'The levels of pests and diseases in our farms have reduced, and our crops are more healthy', and PlantVillage's David Hughes claiming yield increases 'between 130% to 530%'. No peer-reviewed or agency source documents Arisat's case; existing records AIBD-0191 and AIBD-0192 cover Nuru's accuracy study and FAO fall armyworm use.
purpose: Nuru is built to recognize cassava disease and pest symptoms on leaves offline and give management advice; selecting clean cuttings from diagnosed plants is that intended use.
system: PlantVillage Nuru (offline TensorFlow convolutional neural network for cassava disease and pest symptoms on a smartphone)
developer: PlantVillage, Pennsylvania State University, with the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA)
deployer: Lead-farmer program in Busia County run with Self Help Africa and Ugunja Resource Center
taxonomy_note: Knowledge discovery because the stated mechanism is the farmer learning which plants are diseased so as to replant clean cuttings. Written as 'benefit created' because the developer's post describes one farmer's dated, quantified change, but every depth is null: the only account of Arisat is PlantVillage's own, republished through a CGIAR partner page, with confounders (certified seed from 2016, spacing, a buyer aggregation from 2019) that the post does not separate, and the earlier verifier found no peer-reviewed or agency source for any individual farmer.

ratings.reason: Arisat's reported rise from 0.5 kg to 2.0-5.0 kg per plant comes only from the developer's blog, which also records seed, spacing and market changes over the same years.

ai_role.statement: Only the maker's account exists for this case: PlantVillage's post attributes the yield change to Nuru's leaf-scanning diagnosis guiding removal of diseased plants and selection of clean cuttings, in the farmer's words. The independent evidence fetched concerns the model's accuracy (Mrisho et al. 2020, developer co-authored) and another farmer's self-report in Business Insider, not Arisat, so the AI's share of her outcome cannot be assessed.
